newsitem.title: BELGIUM: National debt payments at record high in the EU.
newsitem.headline: National debt payments at record high in the EU.

text.p: The debt burden of European Union countries increased steadily to a record 11 percent of annual public spending by 1995, with Belgium, Italy and Denmark paying the highest cost.
This was the gloomy picture painted by the EU's statistical office Eurostat in a report on interest payments and government expenditure between 1980 and 1995 released on Tuesday.

Debt interest in all the EU states except Greece and Luxembourg totalled 362 billion European currency units ($409 billion) in 1996, 47 percent of which were paid by the governments of Italy (28 percent) and Germany (19 percent), the report said.

Belgium recorded the highest payments per capita at 1,760 ecus, closely followed by Italy on 1,710 ecus and Denmark on 1,700. Portugal had the lowest interest payments per capita in 1996 at 410 Ecus ahead of Britain on 540 ecus.
Eurostat said debt servicing in the 13 EU states represented 11 percent of government spending in 1995 -- the last year for which the calculation was available -- up from 7.0 percent in 1980.

"Growth in government debt has limited the room for manoeuvre in government expenditure. In Belgium and Italy one-fifth of government expenditure is used to service government debt, while in many other member states the figure is about one-tenth," the report says.
EU states have been at pains to reduce their debt to qualify for the launch of the European single currency -- the euro -- which is due to happen on January 1, 1999.

Belgium and Italy have the largest debts as a percentage of gross domestic product (GDP) with a level estimated at respectively 126.7 percent and 122.4 percent in 1997. This is down from a peak of 136.8 percent for Belgium in 1993 and 125.1 percent for Italy in 1994, according to the Commission's recent economic forecasts.

The Maastricht treaty on economic and monetary union says total government debts must not exceed 60 percent of GDP unless the ratio is sufficiently diminishing and approaching the reference value at a satisfactory pace.
